results.title: Don't Throw Away Your Peach Pits This October! Grow Beautiful Peach Trees in Just 3 Steps
results.description:
DON’T THROW AWAY THAT PEACH PIT THIS OCTOBER! 🍑🌱

That little peach pit you were about to throw in the trash could become your very own peach tree — but only if you give it the right conditions.

In this video, I'll show you the exact 3-step method for growing a peach tree from a pit, including how to choose a good pit, how to give it the cold period it needs to break dormancy, and how to plant and protect it through its first winter and summer.

You'll discover:

🍑 How to choose the best peach pits for growing
❄️ Why peach pits need cold stratification before they sprout
🌱 The natural October planting method
🧊 How to use the refrigerator method when outdoor planting isn't practical
💧 How to avoid the moisture and drainage mistakes that cause pits to rot
🐭 How to protect newly planted pits from mice, squirrels, and other animals
☀️ How much sunlight peach seedlings actually need
🌳 How deep to plant a peach pit for better protection
📈 What realistic germination and seedling growth can look like
✂️ How professional nurseries use peach seedlings as rootstock
🍑 Why a seed-grown peach may not produce exactly the same fruit as the parent tree
❄️ And the golden tip about chill hours that can determine whether your future peach tree actually performs well in your climate

The biggest mistake is thinking that peach pits simply need to be buried in soil and watered. They don't work like ordinary seeds. A peach pit has a built-in dormancy system, and winter's cold, moist conditions are part of what tells the seed that it's safe to wake up and grow.

The best part? You don't need expensive equipment or a nursery full of trees. With a few good pits, the right timing, well-drained soil, protection from rodents, and patience, you can start your own peach seedlings from fruit you already enjoyed.

And before you plant, there's one thing you absolutely need to check: the chill requirement of the peach tree the pit came from. Matching that requirement to your local winter can save you years of growing a tree that struggles to bloom or fruit properly.

If you've ever tried growing a peach tree from a pit and failed, this video will show you what may have gone wrong.

🍑 Plant the pit instead of throwing it away. Your future orchard could start this October.

results.title: The AMISH Way to Grow Peaches From Seed — Get Your Own Peach Tree at Home
results.description:
Most people throw the pit of a ripe peach in the compost. Inside that pit is a seed that carries everything needed to grow a peach tree that will produce fruit for twenty-five years.
 
Growing a peach from seed is not difficult. It is not mysterious. The pit from any ripe local peach, prepared correctly and given the right conditions, will germinate and grow into a producing tree. The tree will not produce the exact same variety as the peach you ate — peach seeds are genetically diverse and the result is a surprise. But that surprise is the point. You are growing something entirely new, descended from good genetics, unique to your property and your climate.
 
Our neighbor Mr. Caruso has a peach tree in his yard that produces the finest peach in Lancaster County. That tree was grown from the seed of a peach his wife brought from her family's farm forty years ago. Nobody knows the variety. Nobody needs to know. The tree produced something extraordinary by accident of genetics and it has been producing for forty years.
 
In this video, Elias Yoder — who farms in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania — gives you the complete method for growing a peach from seed. Why the seed requires stratification — the cold period that simulates winter — and how to do it in your refrigerator. Choosing the right peach to save from — local farm varieties for local climate genetics. Cleaning and drying the pit correctly. The fourteen-week refrigerator method. Planting when the root emerges. The south wall position through the first summer. Removing flowers in years one and two to build the root system. The open vase pruning in year two. Year three — the first flowers and the first allowed fruit. The moment of discovery when you taste what the pit contained. And the honest account of what seed-grown trees can become and occasionally do become.

results.title: How to Grow Apricot and Peach Trees From Seed
results.description:
How to Grow Apricot and Peach from Seed, with Katia Plant Scientist 

Have you ever eaten a delicious apricot (Prunus armeniaca) or peach (Prunus persica) and wondered if you could grow a new tree from the pit? Learn with me, Dr. Katia Hougaard, as I guide you through the steps from pit to seedling tree using scientific principles and simple supplies found in most kitchens. 

A note of caution before growing a fruit tree from a pit – some varieties of fruit trees do not “breed true”. Through the genetic reshuffling of sexual reproduction, the offspring of a tree with delicious fruit may not be quite the same as their parent tree. However, the apricot and peach pits I am working with in this video were from self-pollinated heirloom varieties, so they are more likely to “breed true”. 

The first step is to break open the pit or at least break off part of the pit. This allows water to reach the kernel and stimulate germination, while also making it easier for the embryonic root or “radicle” to break out of the shell. Next, the kernel or broken pit is soaked in warm water overnight to ensure it is thoroughly soaked.  

From there, the kernel or broken pit is placed in a loosely sealed plastic bag. Covering the kernel or broken pits in damp paper towels or coco coir helps keep them moist during cold stratification. Cold stratification is the process of “tricking” the seed into thinking it is enduring winter conditions with the aim of beginning germination in the spring. The bag is placed in a fridge at approximately 4 C for two to three months. 

After this time, the seeds may begin germinating. This is visually apparent when long white “tails” appear from the pits. These are the radicles. Even if no visible signs of germination are present, it is still a good idea to remove the pits from cold stratification after two to three months.  

The pits can be placed directly in pots filled with well-drained potting compost, or they can be split open to remove the kernels. Long exposure to moisture can cause the pits to split apart to reveal the kernels. The pits or kernels should be planted approximately 5 centimeters deep. If successful, seedlings should emerge one to two weeks after planting.
